subject: social_science
chapter_title: The Age of Industrialisation: Factories, Workers and Colonies

concepts.title: Proto-Industrialisation before Factories
concepts.definition: Proto-industrialisation was the stage when large-scale production for an international market happened in countryside households with hand tools, not in factories, as merchants supplied rural families with raw material and collected the finished goods.
concepts.key_idea: Peasants took up manufacturing in spare months because open fields and common lands were closing down, and income from such work supplemented their shrinking farm plots.
question_patterns: what is meant by proto industrialisation
why did peasants in the countryside take up proto industrial production
how did merchants control rural production before factories
why did part of europe shift production to the countryside
how was proto industrial production organised
what is the difference between proto industry and factory industry

solution_steps.explain: Check that goods were made in village homes with hand tools rather than in factories.
Merchants moved from town to countryside, supplied money and raw material, and bought the finished cloth for export.
Confirm the closing of open fields and the search for supplementary income drew peasant families into manufacturing.

concepts.title: Cotton Boom, Inventions and the Cotton Mill
concepts.definition: Cotton led the industrial era: Britain's raw cotton imports jumped from 2.5 million pounds in 1760 to 22 million pounds in 1787 as inventions in carding, twisting, spinning and rolling raised each worker's output, and Richard Arkwright's cotton mill gathered costly machines under one roof.
concepts.key_idea: The mill replaced dispersed household cloth production with monitored factory work powered by water and later steam.
question_patterns: why is cotton called the first symbol of the new era
how did britain's raw cotton imports change between 1760 and 1787
which inventions increased the efficacy of the production process
what did richard arkwright create and why does it matter
how did the cotton mill change cloth production
name the steps of cloth production improved by new machines

solution_steps.explain: Cotton imports rose from 2.5 million pounds in 1760 to 22 million pounds by 1787, a near tenfold surge.
Inventions speeded carding, twisting, spinning and rolling, giving stronger threads and yarn with more output per worker.
Arkwright's cotton mill centralised costly machines, supervision and power, replacing dispersed household production.

concepts.title: Growth of Raw Cotton Imports
concepts.definition: The surge in Britain's cotton industry can be measured by the difference between raw cotton imported in an early year and a later year, which shows how quickly the new machines multiplied demand.
concepts.key_idea: Between 1760 and 1787, imports climbed from 2.5 to 22 million pounds, so the added imports capture the scale of the cotton boom.
question_patterns: calculate the increase in britain's raw cotton imports between two years
how many extra million pounds of cotton were imported by 1787
find the rise in imports when the two yearly figures are given
compute the change in raw cotton imports over a period
how fast did britain's cotton demand grow in the late eighteenth century

solution_steps.explain: Take the later year's import and subtract the earlier year's import to get the increase

concepts.title: Slow Adoption of the Steam Engine
concepts.definition: Even the celebrated steam engine spread slowly: James Watt patented his improved engine in 1781, yet at the start of the nineteenth century England had no more than 321 steam engines, with 80 in cotton and nine in wool and the rest in mining, canals and iron works.
concepts.key_idea: Cheap labour and abundant hand skills kept manufacturers from buying costly machines, so technology's triumph was neither sudden nor universal.
question_patterns: why did manufacturers hesitate to adopt the steam engine
how many steam engines were there in england at the beginning of the nineteenth century
where were the earliest steam engines used
who improved and patented the steam engine and when
why did hand labour remain preferred over machines
what does the slow spread of steam power tell us about industrialisation

solution_steps.explain: Watt improved Newcomen's engine, patented it in 1781, and Boulton manufactured the model.
Only 321 engines existed in England around 1800: 80 in cotton, 9 in wool, the remainder in mining, canals and iron works.
Machines were costly, needed repair, and offered no big gains where workers were plentiful and wages low.

concepts.title: Steam Engines outside Cotton and Wool
concepts.definition: Engines not used in the cotton and wool industries went into mining, canal works and iron works, so their number equals the total engines minus those in the two textile trades.
concepts.key_idea: Of the 321 early steam engines, subtracting 80 cotton and 9 wool engines shows over two hundred were working in mines, canals and ironworks.
question_patterns: calculate how many steam engines worked outside the textile industries
how many engines were used in mining canals and iron works
find the engines not used in cotton and wool industries
compute the share of steam engines in non textile sectors
where were most steam engines deployed in early industrial england

solution_steps.explain: Take the total number of steam engines and subtract those in cotton and those in wool industries

concepts.title: Life of Workers and Resistance to Machines
concepts.definition: Workers streamed into towns on rumours of work, relied on kin and jobbers for jobs, and feared that machines like the Spinning Jenny of 1764 would steal their livelihood, as when colliers' wives marched in 1790 to cut up spinning engines.
concepts.key_idea: Wages rose over the century, yet work was seasonal and uncertain, and hostility to new machines showed the human cost behind industrial progress.
question_patterns: why did workers resist the introduction of the spinning jenny
how did workers find jobs in industrial towns
what does the 1790 incident of attacking machines show
who devised the spinning jenny and what did it do
describe the life of industrial workers in the nineteenth century
why was employment uncertain for factory workers

solution_steps.explain: Workers depended on friends, relatives and jobbers who promised work in exchange for favours.
Hand spinners and woollen workers saw machines like the Spinning Jenny cutting demand for manual labour.
Confirm the magistrate's 1790 report of colliers and their wives threatening to cut machines to pieces.

concepts.title: The Age of Indian Textiles and the Gomastha System
concepts.definition: India dominated international textile markets through networks of Armenian and Persian merchants, brokers and supply merchants, until the East India Company tightened control by appointing gomasthas, or paid supervisors, to regulate weavers and cut their ties with other buyers.
concepts.key_idea: Gomasthas advanced loans to weavers who had to sell only to the company at low prices, and punishments and loss of land turned many weavers into rebels or deserters.
question_patterns: how did the east india company procure cotton and silk textiles in india
what was the role of the gomastha
why did weavers resent the company's system of advances
describe the network of merchants and brokers in indian textile trade
how did indian merchants lose control of the textile export trade
what happened to weavers who tried to refuse company loans

solution_steps.explain: Financiers, supply merchants and brokers linked inland weavers to Gulf, Red Sea and Masulipatam ports.
Paid company agents advanced cash, monitored weaving, and stopped weavers from selling to rival buyers.
Loan dependence, price cutting and confiscation of looms drove resistance and migrations.

concepts.title: Manchester Comes to India and Factories Come Up
concepts.definition: Manchester machine-made cloth flooded Indian markets through the 19th century, crushing handloom exports and pushing Indian merchants to shift capital into factories, where early cotton and jute mills came up in Bombay and Bengal.
concepts.key_idea: As imports surged, Indian weavers lost distant markets first and local markets next, and merchants' capital found its way into mill industries.
question_patterns: how did manchester imports affect indian weavers
why did indian merchants begin to invest in factories
where did the first cotton and jute mills come up in india
what changed in the pattern of indian trade in the nineteenth century
how did the civil war in america help indian cotton exports
describe the shift from export trade to mill industry in india

solution_steps.explain: Cheap Manchester cloth captured Indian markets, and tariff policy kept it flowing.
Shut out of export trade, merchants moved money into mill ventures in Bombay and Bengal.
Confirm the first mills: cotton in Bombay from the 1850s and jute in Bengal around the same period.

concepts.title: Peculiarities of Indian Industrial Growth and the Jobber
concepts.definition: Indian industrialisation grew unevenly: mill industries concentrated in a few sectors and regions, factory workers were recruited through jobbers who charged for favours, and most workers came from nearby districts and kept village links.
concepts.key_idea: European managing agencies controlled much of the capital, and Indian entrepreneurs prospered where wartime demand and import gaps opened space.
question_patterns: what were the peculiarities of indian industrial growth
who was a jobber and how did he recruit workers
why is indian industrialisation called uneven
what was the role of european managing agencies in india
from where did factory workers in india come
how did the first world war help indian industries

solution_steps.explain: Note the concentration in cotton, jute and later iron and steel, with few other industries.
Jobbers got trusties from their own villages, often demanding gifts or money for securing jobs.
British mills turned to war needs, letting Indian mills supply home markets and expand during the First World War.

concepts.title: Market for Goods: Advertising and Labels
concepts.definition: Manufacturers sold goods in expanding markets through labels, calendars, newspaper advertisements and images of gods, famous persons and nationalist icons, which built brand recognition among buyers who could not read.
concepts.key_idea: Figures like Lakshmi on soap packets or images of emperors and nawabs on calendars linked products to respectability, and India-made goods wore the nationalist message of swadeshi.
question_patterns: how did manufacturers advertise goods in the age of industrialisation
why were calendars used to sell products
what role did images of gods play in advertising
how did labels help buyers who could not read
what does the use of nationalist messages in advertisements show
describe the calendar advertisements of indian mills

solution_steps.explain: Labels on cloth bundles, street calendars, newspapers and hoardings carried product images to buyers.
Gods, historic figures and beauties gave products respectability and recognition beyond literacy.
Indian mill cloth used nationalist imagery to urge buyers to choose swadeshi goods over Manchester imports.
